title: The Incentive

jokes.text: Kevin responding to a normal workplace question with 'Me do it now. Go. Stop worry'
jokes.setup: A coworker asks Kevin about paperwork in a normal office context
jokes.punchline: Kevin responds in caveman-speak, treating a routine question with prehistoric grammar
jokes.explanation: The absurdity of Kevin's caveman-speak is rooted entirely in his established character as the office's lovable dimwit. The joke lands because the contrast between professional office setting and prehistoric grammar is sharp and specific to Kevin. Good economy — no wasted words.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Me feel good. Body strong. Sleep big last night.'
jokes.setup: Coworkers ask if Kevin feels okay, expecting a normal answer
jokes.punchline: Kevin doubles down on caveman-speak with 'Body strong. Sleep big last night' — the escalation of the grammar gimmick into physical self-assessment
jokes.explanation: 'Sleep big last night' is a particularly funny construction — the word 'big' applied to sleep is unexpected and specific. The escalation of the bit earns an additional laugh beyond the initial caveman conceit.

jokes.text: Oscar's intellectual over-analysis: 'He's making a statement. It's an ironic comment on our expectations of him. A funhouse image of our model of Kevin.'
jokes.setup: Coworkers are alarmed by Kevin's deteriorating speech; Oscar offers an explanation
jokes.punchline: Oscar's pompous pseudo-intellectual defense of Kevin's caveman talk as performance art — the joke is that Oscar is so pretentious he'd rather ascribe high theory than accept the obvious
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. 'A funhouse image of our model of Kevin' is a genuinely clever line — the phrase is internally coherent as art criticism and completely absurd as a description of Kevin grunting. Only Oscar, the office's self-appointed intellectual, would reach this hard for a dignified explanation of something this stupid. The callback potential ('You keep think that' as Kevin's dismissal) makes it even better. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Kevin's deadpan dismissal of Oscar's theory: 'You keep think that.'
jokes.setup: Oscar has just delivered an elaborate intellectual defense of Kevin's speech
jokes.punchline: Kevin — in caveman-speak — casually dismisses it, which is itself funnier in caveman grammar
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum comedy. The joke works on multiple levels: Kevin's caveman-speak punctures Oscar's pretension, Kevin's dismissal in broken grammar is itself a demonstration of his point, and 'You keep think that' is a perfect construction — funnier than 'You keep thinking that' would ever be. Exceptional economy. Among the best lines in the cold open.

jokes.text: Kevin's mechanic analogy: 'Me mechanic not speak English but he know what me mean when me say Car no go. And we best friends.'
jokes.setup: Kevin is defending his stripped-down communication style
jokes.punchline: Kevin's earnest philosophical defense of linguistic minimalism via an imaginary mechanic friendship — the warmth of 'And we best friends' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: Kevin's logic is internally consistent and absurdly earnest. 'Car no go' is a funny reduction. 'And we best friends' lands because it's a non-sequitur emotional payoff — Kevin's argument for efficiency ends in a sweet, off-topic declaration. Good character work.

jokes.text: Andy's warning: 'basically the speech equivalent to just wearing underpants'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining to Kevin that they have a 'word code' like a dress code
jokes.punchline: The metaphor lands: speaking in minimal words is like showing up to work in just your underwear — functional but completely inappropriate
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed analogy that's both apt and funny. The dress code parallel is elegant writing — it makes logical sense and produces a comic image simultaneously. The underpants specificity ('not naked, just underpants') adds a precise comedic layer.

jokes.text: Kevin: 'Many small time make big time.'
jokes.setup: Andy argues Kevin is only saving a 'microscopic amount of time' with his word-reduction strategy
jokes.punchline: Kevin's caveman-grammatical rebuttal is also a genuinely sound economic principle — delivered with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: Funny because Kevin's broken aphorism actually makes sense. The joke is that he's accidentally correct while sounding ridiculous. Economy score is near-perfect — five words, complete comic idea.

jokes.text: Andy: 'What are you going to do with all this time?' Kevin: 'See world.'
jokes.setup: Andy sarcastically asks what grand plans Kevin has for all the time he's saving
jokes.punchline: Kevin's ambition: 'See world' — which sounds either like global travel or SeaWorld, both equally absurd for Kevin
jokes.explanation: The ambiguity is the joke — and it's planted perfectly for the SeaWorld payoff that follows. Kevin's grandiose answer ('see world') is also deflating: the biggest possible ambition stated in the most reductive way. The layered misdirection is a mark of good writing.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Kevin, are you saying "see the world" or SeaWorld?'
jokes.setup: Kevin says 'See world' as his life ambition enabled by word-saving
jokes.punchline: Andy clocks the homophone ambiguity — is Kevin dreaming of global travel, or a Florida theme park?
jokes.explanation: This is a perfectly constructed wordplay joke that earns its laughs. The setup was invisible — 'See world' sounded like world travel — and the realization that it might be SeaWorld is both funnier AND more Kevin-appropriate. The ambiguity is resolved (or not resolved) beautifully.

jokes.text: Kevin clarifies: 'See world. Oceans. Fish Jump. China.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks if Kevin means 'see the world' or 'SeaWorld'
jokes.punchline: Kevin's answer ('Oceans. Fish Jump. China.') only deepens the ambiguity — fish jumping could be SeaWorld shows; China could be the country or... a ceramic exhibit
jokes.explanation: The joke escalates perfectly. 'Fish Jump' is delightful — it sounds like a SeaWorld show AND describes the ocean. 'China' is the killer: does Kevin mean the country (globe-spanning travel) or is this still somehow SeaWorld-adjacent? The construction leaves the ambiguity gloriously unresolved, which is funnier than any clean answer would be. Maximum economy, maximum absurdity. One of the best jokes in the episode.

jokes.text: Kevin's talking head: 'When me president they see.' — then cuts to Kevin sitting in silence for 5 seconds.
jokes.setup: Kevin is delivering a defiant talking-head confessional about his future ambitions
jokes.punchline: His presidential threat trails off into ambiguous silence — the camera holds on him and he offers nothing more, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: The talking head is perfectly structured: Kevin's caveman grammar + grandiose political ambition + the beat of silence after 'They see' adds up to pure comedy. The unfinished threat ('They see... [what?]') is funnier for being incomplete. The pause is the punchline. Justifies the 8 — it's a classically constructed Office talking head beat.

jokes.text: The Sabre Pyramid tablet: absurd weight, battery pack requirements, and memory measured in 'L' (a unit nobody recognizes)
jokes.setup: Dwight presents the new Sabre tablet, the 'Pyramid,' as a revolutionary product
jokes.punchline: It's revealed to be a comically impractical device — weighing a ton with battery pack, having memory measured in an invented unit ('50 L'), and Dwight's only advice being 'You're really going to want the booster'
jokes.explanation: The 'L' memory unit is the best gag here — the escalating incomprehensibility of the specs (How many I to a K?) is a running joke on corporate jargon and tech buzzwords. Competent satire but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Andy interrupting Dwight's meeting about a failing product to ask about tie clips and calling Jim 'C-Span'
jokes.setup: Dwight is in the middle of a product meeting; Andy bursts in with a completely unrelated personal concern
jokes.punchline: Andy hijacks the meeting to ask about tie choices, demonstrating his total managerial incompetence while calling it 'pulling rank'
jokes.explanation: Good character work for Andy — his insecurity about Robert's first impression driving him to derail a product meeting is classic. The 'C-Span' nickname is a reach but the explanation ('Cocker spaniel because of your Spanish bloodline...') at least commits to the bit.

jokes.text: Andy explains 'C-Span' = Cocker Spaniel, 'Spaniel because of your Spanish bloodline, Cocker because—' [cut off]
jokes.setup: Jim asks what 'C-Span' means
jokes.punchline: Andy's etymology reveals 'Cocker' is clearly going somewhere inappropriate, and the scene cuts before he can finish — the implication is the joke
jokes.explanation: The cut before 'Cocker because—' is well-timed. The audience fills in the blank. It's a standard joke structure but executed cleanly. Andy's obliviousness to why this is inappropriate adds to the character comedy.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head: 'Here's how I'm going to help out from now on. I'm going to not care. And I'm going to sit around quietly waiting for Andy's inevitable demise.'
jokes.setup: Andy has just hijacked Dwight's meeting and called it 'pulling rank'
jokes.punchline: Dwight's confessional reveals his 'strategy' — passive aggressive non-participation, delivered with his characteristic absolute conviction
jokes.explanation: 'Inevitable demise' is a great Dwight phrase — grandiose and specific. The joke is that Dwight's 'help' is explicitly the opposite of helping, stated as a formal plan. Pure character comedy that requires no setup beyond knowing who Dwight is.

jokes.text: Robert California referring to Jim as 'Your friend Neil Patrick Harris' to Andy
jokes.setup: Robert California is talking to Andy about something
jokes.punchline: Robert describes Jim only as 'your friend Neil Patrick Harris' — a bizarre celebrity comparison delivered with total sincerity as if it's obviously correct
jokes.explanation: Pure Robert California character comedy. The joke is that Robert operates in his own associative universe — Jim made him laugh, therefore Jim = Neil Patrick Harris. The specificity of the celebrity choice and the matter-of-fact delivery are what make it work. Only Robert would say this.

jokes.text: The nickname chain: Erin calls Andy 'D Dog,' Andy approves it, tells Erin she's 'E Dog,' the whole office adopts dog names
jokes.setup: Erin calls Andy 'D Dog' because Andy wants everyone to use his new nickname to impress Robert
jokes.punchline: The absurd corporate formality of 'Andy wants us to' plus the immediate embrace of 'P Dog' for Phyllis creates a ridiculous nickname ecosystem
jokes.explanation: Functional humor. The escalation of everyone getting dog names is a mild joke — it works but doesn't have a particularly sharp punchline beyond the absurdity of the situation.

jokes.text: Andy describing sleeping with his ex-wife: 'Yeah, we had a few fights I suppose, but last night we put a lot of that to bed.'
jokes.setup: Andy is describing his improved relationship with his ex-wife
jokes.punchline: 'Put a lot of that to bed' is a double entendre — it means resolved, but also literally went to bed together, which the next lines will confirm
jokes.explanation: A competent double entendre. The 'put it to bed' phrase is slightly too obvious as a setup for what follows, but the delivery carries it.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I can't tell you what I did with my ex-wife last night. I have to sing it.' — then sings about their shower together
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining he slept with his ex-wife; he says he 'can't tell' the story
jokes.punchline: He then sings it — 'We took a shower / We were naked / We...' — which is Andy's specific character tic (his need to perform) making an already awkward overshare even more uncomfortable
jokes.explanation: The joke is elevated entirely by character integration. Andy's compulsive need to sing rather than speak, applied to a sexually uncomfortable overshare about his ex-wife, is perfectly Andy. 'We were naked / We...' trailing off mid-song is both the cringe and the punchline. Only Andy Bernard would do this. The interruption by his father walking in makes it even better.

jokes.text: Andy's father walks in mid-song, just as Andy is singing about being naked with his ex-wife
jokes.setup: Andy is singing about showering naked with his ex-wife to a room full of coworkers
jokes.punchline: His father walks through the door at precisely 'We were naked / We...' — the cringe escalation reaches maximum embarrassment
jokes.explanation: The timing of the father's entrance is the joke — perfect sitcom structure. It's not the most original comedic device but the execution is clean. The silent 'Oh, hi Dad' reaction beat compounds the cringe. Impact score is high because a room full of viewers would audibly react.

jokes.text: 'Oh. Hi, Dad. Oh, boy.' — someone walks in while Andy is mid-song about his sex life
jokes.setup: Andy is singing explicit details about his night with his ex-wife
jokes.punchline: A family member (his father?) walks in — the audience/coworkers witness this; Andy's 'Oh, boy' confirms the horror
jokes.explanation: A solid cringe button on the singing sequence. The 'Hi, Dad' reveal is a classic comedy escalation — the stakes of the oversharing suddenly get higher. 'Oh, boy' is a perfect Andy reaction (understated, slightly defeated). Not the most original construction but executed well.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'Andy, do you know why I chose you? I think I can sum it up with what I think is your favorite ice cream flavor.' Andy: 'Vanilla?' Robert: 'Vanilla? No.'
jokes.setup: Robert is building to an inspiring speech about why he chose Andy; Andy tries to guess his own flavor
jokes.punchline: Andy guesses vanilla — the most boring possible answer — and Robert is genuinely startled and dismissive: 'Vanilla? No.' The horror in his 'No' is the joke
jokes.explanation: Two-word punchline: 'Vanilla? No.' Robert's dismissal is perfectly in character — he sees himself as a man of sophisticated taste, and Andy guessing vanilla is an affront. But the meta-joke is that Andy IS vanilla — the boring, safe choice — which makes Robert's denial even funnier. Only Robert California would open an inspirational speech by speculating about ice cream. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Robert: 'You'll never guess in a million billion years you'll never guess.' Andy: 'You were saying you chose me. There was a reason.'
jokes.setup: Robert is building suspense about Andy's ice cream flavor/his reason for choosing Andy
jokes.punchline: Robert gets lost in his own game; Andy has to gently redirect him back to the actual topic ('There was a reason') — deflating Robert's theatrics with gentle practicality
jokes.explanation: Good Robert character comedy — he gets so absorbed in his own riddles he forgets the point. Andy's straight-man 'There was a reason' is the kind of deflation that works in a two-shot. Slightly undercut by the scene moving on before the ice cream flavor is ever revealed.

jokes.text: Andy serving Robert a freezing cup of old coffee and drinking it himself: 'I've been craving a freezing cup of old coffee. Mmm.'
jokes.setup: Erin serves Robert cold, old coffee by mistake; Andy intercepts to save face
jokes.punchline: Andy claims the old cold coffee is what HE wanted and commits to drinking it with performative enthusiasm ('Mmm') to cover the error
jokes.explanation: Andy's people-pleasing anxiety driving him to drink terrible coffee and pretend to love it is a solid cringe beat. 'I've been craving a freezing cup of old coffee' is a funny line. Well-executed but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Robert to Jim: 'I'm afraid you've lost my interest. Let me call you back. I got to go.' — hanging up mid-sentence
jokes.setup: Jim is telling Robert about his romantic situation — 'we're in this weird dance and now we're...'
jokes.punchline: Robert simply declares he's lost interest, mid-call, and hangs up — no apology, no social nicety, complete Robert California sociopathic bluntness
jokes.explanation: Perfect Robert California. The line 'I'm afraid you've lost my interest' is his character distilled — he says aloud what everyone thinks but never says, with the politeness of 'I'm afraid' making the ruthlessness even funnier. Hanging up immediately after is the physical commitment. Highly quotable. Justifies the 8+.

jokes.text: Robert's motivational speech: 'If the office superstore was supposed to put us little suppliers out of business, why are we still here?'
jokes.setup: Robert is attempting to motivate the sales team
jokes.punchline: Jim quietly answers 'Yeah' to the rhetorical question — and Robert's response ('You'd go someplace else? That's not it. That's not the answer. There are no wrong answers.') reveals the salespeople are completely unmoved by this speech
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Robert's grandiose motivational speech is met with genuine confusion rather than inspiration. 'There are no wrong answers' after declaring someone's answer wrong is a nice ironic touch. Competent but not a standout.

jokes.text: Robert's motivational speech: 'If the office superstore was supposed to put us little suppliers out of business, why are we still here?' — followed by uncomfortable silence, then: 'Yeah. This is where we go.'
jokes.setup: Robert poses a rhetorical question to the sales team about why they've survived.
jokes.punchline: Jim gives a wrong answer. Robert confirms it's wrong but then says 'There are no wrong answers' — before immediately contradicting that by saying 'It's a wrong answer.' The pseudo-Socratic corporate speech collapses under its own contradictions.
jokes.explanation: The 'no wrong answers / it's a wrong answer' contradiction is a solid laugh. Robert's inspirational corporate speak being simultaneously vague and self-contradicting is good character work. The pauses and rhythm make this scene work more on screen than on paper.

jokes.text: Andy: 'You got it. Double.' Robert: 'Done.' Andy: 'I'm not kidding.' Robert: 'Neither am I.' Andy: 'It's already done.' [pause] 'I'm just kidding. It's going to take some time. Double.'
jokes.setup: Robert has challenged Andy to double sales; Andy keeps eagerly agreeing faster and faster, then realizes he overcommitted
jokes.punchline: 'I'm just kidding. It's going to take some time.' — Andy's bravado collapses into honesty in real time
jokes.explanation: A good Andy moment. The rapid escalation ('Done' / 'I'm not kidding' / 'Neither am I' / 'It's already done') mimics the rhythm of a negotiation where both parties keep raising stakes neither can cash, then Andy's immediate deflation is very true to his character. The final 'Double' — restating the goal after admitting he was kidding — is a nice button.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Double. Done.' Robert: 'I'm not kidding.' Andy: 'Neither am I. It's already done.' [beat] 'I'm just kidding. It's going to take some time. Double.'
jokes.setup: Robert has just told Andy to double the office's best sales numbers. Andy confidently says it's 'already done'
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately folds — 'I'm just kidding. It's going to take some time.' — revealing his bravado was pure panic, and he has no plan
jokes.explanation: Great Andy character beat. The bravado-to-collapse arc is rapid and true to the character — he says 'Done' with total conviction and then immediately panics and walks it back. The rhythm of 'Neither am I. It's already done. [pause] I'm just kidding' is well-structured. Could only be Andy.

jokes.text: Andy's 'rap session' — gathering the team for a 'little rap session to talk about business' that has no agenda and no ideas
jokes.setup: Andy has promised Robert to double sales; he calls a team meeting
jokes.punchline: The meeting is completely empty — Andy has no plan, just buzzwords ('summon that') and eventually asks for ideas while having none himself
jokes.explanation: The scene captures the comedy of a leaderless meeting well. 'You have to summon that' as a response to 'how do we double sales' is a good empty-manager line. Not a standout scene but functionally funny throughout.

jokes.text: Andy's 'rap session' with the salespeople: 'Just thought we'd have a little rap session. Talk about business. See how things are going.' followed by awkward silence.
jokes.setup: Andy calls an informal meeting, referring to it as a 'rap session.'
jokes.punchline: The casual management-speak ('rap session') combined with nobody saying anything creates an awkward void that exposes Andy's lack of actual leadership substance.
jokes.explanation: Functional cringe setup. The term 'rap session' is mildly amusing but the beat works better as setup for the subsequent jokes than as a standalone moment.

jokes.text: Darryl: 'I was just thinking about Robert. Man, what a boss. Just throws down goals, you know?' — clearly sycophantic with nothing of substance to add
jokes.setup: Andy asks the group to start a discussion; Darryl jumps in enthusiastically
jokes.punchline: Darryl's contribution is pure empty praise — he's learned to say things that sound engaged while contributing nothing — which is ironic given his intelligence
jokes.explanation: Darryl playing office politics by praising Robert vacuously is a good character note, but it's subtle enough to land as a mild chuckle rather than a genuine laugh. Works in context.

jokes.text: Jim: 'If we could just double our sales, we already would have.' Oscar: 'You're not making any sense.' Jim: 'He brings up two good points.'
jokes.setup: Andy tells the team they need to 'summon' the ability to double sales
jokes.punchline: Jim's perfectly reasonable logic ('we would have already if we could') is called nonsensical; Jim then credits Oscar for making 'two good points' — meaning Jim agrees with both Oscar's critique of Jim AND Jim's original statement
jokes.explanation: 'He brings up two good points' is a genuinely clever line — Jim casually validating both his own argument and Oscar's critique of his argument simultaneously, with perfect deadpan. Classic Jim Halpert comedy: the smart guy playing dumb while exposing everyone else's absurdity.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'We could talk about how fast children grow up and before you know it they're out of the house.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asking the sales team for actual ideas to double revenue; Dwight has pledged to be unhelpful
jokes.punchline: Dwight's 'contribution' to a business strategy meeting is a musing about the passage of childhood — completely irrelevant, delivered as if it's a viable option
jokes.explanation: This is the payoff to Dwight's earlier confessional about refusing to help Andy. The non-sequitur is perfectly timed and utterly in Dwight's register — it sounds like something Dwight would ponder seriously. The callback makes it land harder than the line alone would.

jokes.text: Jim's 'Tuna' and 'Fart' contributions — sitting at the meeting but reducing his input to single random words: 'Tuna.' ... 'Fart.'
jokes.setup: Andy is asking for new leads, territories, big clients — real business proposals
jokes.punchline: Jim's responses to each request: 'Tuna.' and 'Fart.' — monosyllabic sabotage delivered deadpan, possibly referencing the Kevin cold open's word-economy bit
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'Tuna' and 'Fart' are a perfect callback to Kevin's philosophy of saving words — Jim is doing it ironically, in a business meeting, and the escalation from 'Tuna' to 'Fart' is its own mini-escalation. The economy score is a 10: two words, two laughs, perfect structure. 'Good sesh' from Andy to close the scene is the cherry on top.

jokes.text: Andy wraps up the pointless meeting with 'Good sesh' and someone says 'That leg's asleep'
jokes.setup: The meeting has produced nothing — 'Tuna,' a story about children growing up, 'Fart'
jokes.punchline: 'Good sesh' — Andy declares the useless meeting a success; the 'That leg's asleep' suggests someone was so bored they went numb
jokes.explanation: 'Good sesh' is an Andy-specific bit of false positivity. The leg being asleep is a nice physical comedy implication — the meeting was so inert someone literally fell asleep sitting still. Functional button on the scene.

jokes.text: Val catching Darryl apparently faxing (or doing something suspicious); his panicked 'Don't—' and disclaimer 'I'm using the fax. This isn't... No, wait. I'm not supposed to represent the company, right?'
jokes.setup: Val comes looking for Darryl and finds him doing something he immediately needs to explain/justify
jokes.punchline: Darryl's panicked non-explanation ('I'm using the fax. This isn't—') implies something far worse than whatever he was actually doing; the more he explains the worse it sounds
jokes.explanation: Solid cringe beat. The implication of something inappropriate vs. the mundane reality (using the fax) works, but without more context from the visual scene it's harder to fully land from transcript alone.

jokes.text: Darryl's new girlfriend Justine mistakes a random person for Darryl at the fax machine; Darryl talking-head: 'Rub a dub, dub, apricot scrub'
jokes.setup: Justine arrives at the office looking for Darryl and approaches a fax machine thinking someone there is Darryl
jokes.punchline: Darryl's confessional response 'Rub a dub, dub, apricot scrub' — a nonsensical happy sing-song that shows he is extremely pleased with himself about this woman
jokes.explanation: 'Rub a dub, dub, apricot scrub' as a confessional beat is an excellent Darryl moment — his happiness is so overwhelming it comes out as nonsense rhyme. It's unexpected, character-specific, and the image of Darryl exuding this much dopamine energy about a woman is funny.

jokes.text: Darryl leading Justine away with: 'I've been thinking about you all morning. I don't know what you did. I can barely walk today.'
jokes.setup: Darryl takes Justine to a private space to talk
jokes.punchline: Darryl's opening line is a flagrant sexual comment said within earshot of his entire office, including people he just introduced her to
jokes.explanation: The cringe comes from Darryl saying something intimate and sexually charged in a professional public setting. 'I can barely walk today' is a funny construction. Decent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Andy to Dwight: 'D Bone, there you are. Let me guess — somebody needs a brownie. Lick the spoon?'
jokes.setup: Andy finds Dwight in what seems to be an eating situation and immediately misreads it
jokes.punchline: Andy's entirely wrong assumption ('needs a brownie / lick the spoon') displays his cluelessness and condescension toward Dwight simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Andy's condescending assumptions about Dwight are a reliable character beat but this particular instance is underdeveloped — the 'brownie/lick the spoon' joke doesn't have a clear target and lands weakly without visual context.

jokes.text: Dwight complaining about profits: 'I just don't see the point. It's so Wall Street.' Andy: 'I know, right? Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks Dwight about their conversation and Dwight deflects with anti-capitalist rhetoric
jokes.punchline: Andy agrees with Dwight's dismissal of profits as 'so Wall Street' — he's so desperate to bond with Dwight he agrees with an opinion that directly undermines his own job
jokes.explanation: The irony of Andy agreeing that profits are 'so Wall Street' is a good character beat — his need for approval overriding his professional responsibilities. Subtle and true to character.

jokes.text: Dwight: 'I made some inroads in salad but heirloom tomatoes are pushing back.'
jokes.setup: Andy asks how everything is going at Schrute Farms
jokes.punchline: Dwight describes the beet market using military/geopolitical language — 'made inroads' and 'pushing back' — as if produce competition is a wartime campaign
jokes.explanation: Classic Dwight. The application of military strategy language to salad competition is perfectly in character — Dwight treats everything as a battle. 'Heirloom tomatoes are pushing back' is a genuinely funny line that could only come from Dwight's worldview. High character integration score is fully earned.

jokes.text: Andy pivots: 'Got to be some way you could double your beet sales.' — applying Robert's impossible target to Dwight's farm as if it's advice, then: 'You wanted the job, the job is yours, just do the job. And I'll do mine.'
jokes.setup: Andy is supposed to be getting wisdom from Dwight; instead he panics and accidentally gives Dwight the same useless advice Robert gave him
jokes.punchline: Andy walks off having contributed nothing, while Dwight offers him a walnut — the whole scene is a comedy of avoidance on both sides
jokes.explanation: The joke is that Andy, under pressure to double sales, starts giving Dwight the same empty directive. Self-referential and character-true. The walnut offer ('Walnuts?' 'No.') is a funny non sequitur button.

jokes.text: Pam showing Jim an issue of Parenting magazine: 'This is CeCe's favorite magazine. She loves the pictures of babies. She looks at it when she's on the potty and she makes the faces.'
jokes.setup: Pam presents a parenting magazine to Jim, seemingly to discuss the articles
jokes.punchline: Pam reveals CeCe uses it as potty-reading material and 'makes the faces' — a specific, funny detail about infant behavior that completely deflates any seriousness about the magazine
jokes.explanation: 'She makes the faces' is the specific comic detail that elevates this — the image of a baby on the potty making strained faces while looking at pictures of other babies is genuinely funny and very specific. Good parental observational humor.

jokes.text: Jim's guilty reaction when Pam asks if he's 'read' the article on walking while pregnant: 'I flipped through it.'
jokes.setup: Pam asks if Jim read the specific article about the importance of walking during pregnancy
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'I flipped through it' — clearly meaning he looked at nothing — then Pam immediately nailing him: 'So you saw the article on...' — and Jim's 'Of course, yeah. We know that.' pre-emptive agreement
jokes.explanation: Relatable domestic comedy — the spouse who says they read something but obviously didn't. Executed cleanly with Jim's immediate capitulation ('Of course, yeah. We know that.') showing practiced survival instincts.

jokes.text: Jim says he always wanted to be thanked for coming into a meeting and never was, so he's going to thank people now.
jokes.setup: Jim thanks everyone for coming to his brainstorming meeting
jokes.punchline: Jim explains his policy: he always wanted to be thanked for attending a meeting so now he does it — a small, specific, oddly poignant office grievance deployed as comedy
jokes.explanation: A sweet, observational beat about office life. More charming than laugh-out-loud funny — the specificity of the grievance works but the joke is mild.

jokes.text: The reveal of Andy's incentive prizes under the blanket — a pile of kids' toys, a vibrator, and random items
jokes.setup: Andy has a blanket-covered table of 'incentives' to boost sales; he dramatically reveals it
jokes.punchline: The assortment is absurd: a polar bear stuffed animal, a vibrator, John Irving collected works — completely random, childlike items mixed with something inappropriate
jokes.explanation: The reveal of the prize table is a strong visual gag. The juxtaposition of kid-oriented rewards (polar bear, points system) with a vibrator is the central joke. The question 'Is that a vibrator?' getting '20 points' as a response is a sharp button.

jokes.text: Oscar's immediate deconstruction: 'It seems like a basic reward system where you give us points and then we redeem those points for prizes.' Andy: 'You're exactly right. And you get a point.'
jokes.setup: Andy is explaining his point system with theatrical buildup
jokes.punchline: Oscar cuts through the mystique immediately with a dry accurate summary; Andy rewards the deflation by immediately deploying the system
jokes.explanation: The joke works on two levels: Oscar's demystification is funny, and Andy immediately giving him a point for saying the obvious is charming. The system eating itself in its first moment of use is good structure.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'Oh. Uh, is that a vibrator?' Andy: '20 points.'
jokes.setup: The prize table has been revealed and people are identifying items
jokes.punchline: Andy sidesteps the question of what a vibrator is doing in his rewards table by treating it as a pointable question ('20 points' for asking it)
jokes.explanation: '20 points' as a non-answer to 'is that a vibrator?' is a beautifully economical joke. Andy instantly deploys the system to avoid addressing the elephant in the room, and 20 points implies the vibrator question is worth more than basic competence but less than something serious. The economy is near-perfect.

jokes.text: Meredith: 'Why is it all kids' stuff and a vibrator? It's so gross.' Andy: 'There's lots of stuff. John Irving, collected works, 22 points.'
jokes.setup: The office is reacting to the bizarre prize collection
jokes.punchline: Andy's defensive pivot to 'John Irving, collected works' as a counterexample — a set of literary novels among sex toys and stuffed animals — makes the collection weirder, not better
jokes.explanation: The John Irving collection as a defense of prize variety is funny because it makes zero sense — collected works of a literary novelist alongside a vibrator and a polar bear somehow makes the catalog worse. Andy's earnest delivery as if this solves the problem is the joke.

jokes.text: Stanley: 'How about you want us to work harder, pay us more.' Andy: 'I can't.'
jokes.setup: Andy has presented his points-for-prizes system as motivation for the team
jokes.punchline: Stanley cuts to the only logical solution ('pay us more') and Andy's flat 'I can't' is the perfect deflation — the whole incentive system is because he literally cannot do the one thing that would work
jokes.explanation: Stanley's blunt practicality puncturing Andy's elaborate system is pure character comedy. 'I can't' as the entirety of Andy's response — no spin, no redirect — is great deadpan. Both characters are perfectly themselves in two exchanges.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I didn't mean to offend you and I hope you'll forgive me because I am very very "sari." 16 points.' [holds up a sari]
jokes.setup: The team complains the points system is insulting; Andy apologizes
jokes.punchline: Andy's pun on 'sorry/sari' while holding up a sari from the prize table — simultaneously deploying the system and making a terrible pun — and then awarding himself 16 points for it
jokes.explanation: The triple-layer joke: bad pun, prop comedy, and self-awarded points all in one move. Andy's earnest delight in his own awful pun is perfect character work. The reaction note (the item is clarified to be a tablecloth) adds another layer. This is the kind of joke that gets better on rewatch.

jokes.text: Someone notes: 'That's a tablecloth.' — correcting Andy's sari
jokes.setup: Andy has theatrically held up what he calls a sari for his pun
jokes.punchline: It's not a sari — it's a tablecloth — meaning Andy's prize table items are not even what he thinks they are
jokes.explanation: Good button on the sari joke. Andy's prize system is so haphazard he doesn't even know what's in it. Three-word punchline ('That's a tablecloth') lands cleanly.

jokes.text: Andy escalating the incentive system: 'For 500 points, I will wear a dress to work.'
jokes.setup: The team isn't excited by the prize table; someone asks what's available for an extreme number of points (500)
jokes.punchline: Andy pivots from external prizes to offering himself as the prize — beginning the escalation that ends in a tattoo
jokes.explanation: The pivot from products to Andy's own body as incentive is a smart structural turn. 'Wear a dress' as the entry-level offer establishes the escalating absurdity to come.

jokes.text: Andy: 'For 1,000 points, I'll run naked through the parking lot with a donut on my ding dong.'
jokes.setup: The team likes the dress offer; someone pushes for 1,000 points
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately has a specific, detailed plan for 1,000-point nudity — 'with a donut on my ding dong' — the specificity is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'With a donut on my ding dong' is the kind of specific, absurd detail that makes a joke memorable. Andy didn't just say 'I'll run naked' — he had an accessory in mind. The childish language ('ding dong') adds to Andy's character. Highly quotable within the episode.

jokes.text: Andy: 'For 5,000 points, I will let you tattoo whatever you want on the stern of the old S.S. Bernard.'
jokes.setup: The escalating self-punishment incentive reaches its peak
jokes.punchline: Andy offers a tattoo — the permanent, irrevocable commitment — while calling his butt 'the stern of the old S.S. Bernard,' a naval metaphor that is specific and revealing
jokes.explanation: 'The stern of the old S.S. Bernard' is a genuinely great line. It's absurdly nautical, uses his actual last name as the ship's name, and treats his buttocks with the dignity of a maritime vessel. Only Andy Bernard would call his ass this. The escalation structure (dress → naked run with donut → tattoo) also peaks perfectly here. Justifies the 8+ score.

jokes.text: Dwight's talking head about Stanley: 'I sat next to Stanley for years and this is nap time. Open eye nap time. He balances the phone on his shoulder and just powers down.'
jokes.setup: Dwight is noting the change in office energy since Andy's incentive announcement
jokes.punchline: 'Open eye nap time' as a specific description of Stanley's work style — and the image of him balancing a phone while unconscious
jokes.explanation: 'Open eye nap time' is a great coined phrase. The specificity of 'balances the phone on his shoulder and just powers down' makes it a genuinely funny observational detail about Stanley — who is famous for his disengagement. Only someone who has sat next to Stanley for years (Dwight) would know this level of operational detail.

jokes.text: Jim's casual revelation: 'Oh, 100%. We all want to see you tattoo your ass.'
jokes.setup: Andy nervously asks Jim if the incentive has something to do with the sudden office energy
jokes.punchline: Jim's completely matter-of-fact confirmation that the entire office motivation is to see Andy get a butt tattoo — delivered without any editorial
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jim delivery. The 'Oh, 100%' opener signals complete confidence before the absurd statement. He says it like someone confirming they want a bagel. The deadpan normalcy applied to 'we all want to see you tattoo your ass' is classic Halpert.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I think people thought I was kidding when I said that.' Jim: 'No. You definitely weren't kidding. That came across loud and clear.'
jokes.setup: Andy desperately hopes the tattoo offer was understood as a joke
jokes.punchline: Jim offers zero comfort — confirming it was crystal clear, with the slightly ominous 'loud and clear' military language
jokes.explanation: Jim's 'That came across loud and clear' is a beautifully understated refusal to help Andy escape. He's not cruel about it — just accurate. The Office's best straight-man work often involves Jim giving someone an honest answer they desperately don't want.

jokes.text: Dwight handing in 120 points: 'Yeah. Big sale. Don't worry about it though. I don't really care about the points. I would like a point receipt though.'
jokes.setup: Dwight has pledged to be unhelpful; he arrives with a massive point submission
jokes.punchline: Dwight claims not to care about the points while immediately requesting a receipt — he cares intensely about the points and is lying to himself and Andy
jokes.explanation: The callback to Dwight's confessional ('I'm going to not care') pays off perfectly. Dwight has made the biggest sale, then denies caring about the reward, then immediately requests documentation of said reward. 'I would like a point receipt though' is a perfect Dwight line — bureaucratic, competitive, and self-deceiving all at once. Justifies the 8+.

jokes.text: Kevin at his desk: 'Hey, Kevin, what are you doing?' Kevin: 'Don't talk to me.'
jokes.setup: Kevin was doing caveman-speak all episode; now someone checks on him
jokes.punchline: Kevin's response is now completely normal — 'Don't talk to me' — but the context of his earlier caveman speech makes even this normal phrase feel like a significant escalation
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback button — Kevin is now in the zone, working hard, and speaking normally. The contrast with his earlier philosophical caveman stance is the joke. He abandoned his word-economy speech in favor of being just irritable. Good structural payoff to the cold open.

jokes.text: Andy calling a professor he found in a management book ('Management' by Professor Frank) to ask about 'de-incentivizing strategies' and describing himself as being in a 'classic ass-tattoo-incentive situation'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to find a way out of his tattoo promise; he cold-calls a management professor
jokes.punchline: 'I guess you could say I'm in one of those classic ass-tattoo-incentive situations' — said with total earnestness, as if this is a recognized management concept
jokes.explanation: 'Classic ass-tattoo-incentive situation' is one of the episode's best lines. The deadpan delivery of a completely insane phrase as if it's established business terminology is absurdist comedy at its best. The detail of the professor's book being called 'Management' is also a quiet joke. The image of Andy cold-calling a management professor for this specific problem is a perfect Andy Bernard moment. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Andy's response to learning the office hit 5,000 points in one day: 'Took 'em one day.'
jokes.setup: Andy hoped the 5,000-point target would take a long time, giving him an escape
jokes.punchline: The office mobilized so completely (motivated purely by the tattoo) that they hit it in a single day — Andy's flat delivery of 'Took 'em one day' is the stunned punchline
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum comedic weight. Andy's dread is perfectly conveyed in the flat delivery — he cannot believe his employees, who won't work for money, will move mountains to see him tattooed. The economy is exceptional.

jokes.text: Andy's car as a prize: 'My car. For 1,000 points. Or best offer.'
jokes.setup: Andy is trying to add new prizes to divert from the tattoo
jokes.punchline: 'Or best offer' — Andy is treating his car like a Craigslist listing in the middle of a professional incentive meeting, implying the prize can be negotiated
jokes.explanation: 'Or best offer' is a perfect three-word joke — the Craigslist language applied to a corporate incentive system reveals Andy's desperation and creates an absurd image. Concise and character-true.

jokes.text: Phyllis's tattoo design: something coming out of a butt — presumably a baby — eliciting 'Oh! So nasty, Phyllis. Oh my God.'
jokes.setup: The office is designing Andy's tattoo; Phyllis presents her idea
jokes.punchline: Phyllis — seemingly sweet — proposes something graphic and disturbing involving a baby emerging from a butt
jokes.explanation: Perfect Phyllis subversion — she appears gentle and then produces the most disturbing proposal in the room. 'So nasty, Phyllis' as the only response is funny because it acknowledges the audience's reaction. The character inversion (sweet Phyllis = most depraved idea) is well-executed dark comedy.

jokes.text: Andy: 'We should think about this. Does anyone have any better ideas?' Everyone: 'I like what we have.' 'Yeah, nice try.'
jokes.setup: Andy hopes someone will suggest an alternative to the baby-from-butt tattoo
jokes.punchline: Universal endorsement of the disgusting design — 'I like what we have' — and 'Nice try' as a knowing dismissal of Andy's attempt to escape
jokes.explanation: 'Nice try' is a good button — it acknowledges the audience knows Andy is stalling. The unanimous endorsement of the gross tattoo shows the office's unified purpose. Functional scene work.

jokes.text: Jim to Andy outside: 'Nobody really expects you to go through with this.'
jokes.setup: Andy is clearly having second thoughts about the tattoo
jokes.punchline: Jim gives apparently reassuring words — then immediately confirms the opposite when Andy asks directly again ('Absolutely not'), setting up the actual reversal: Andy goes through with it
jokes.explanation: Jim's gentle dishonesty (telling Andy what he wants to hear) sets up the reversal. The scene works because the audience knows Jim is wrong — he thinks Andy won't do it, but he will. Solid structural setup.

jokes.text: Andy confessional before the tattoo: 'No one expects me to go through with this, right?' Camera presumably cuts. Beat. Andy: 'Absolutely not.'
jokes.setup: Andy is seeking reassurance that he won't actually have to get the tattoo
jokes.punchline: Andy asks the question and then immediately answers it himself — either talking to the documentary crew who confirm it or answering his own rhetorical question, then marching back in
jokes.explanation: Andy answering his own reassurance-seeking question is a good character beat. The brevity and confidence of 'Absolutely not' after a pause suggests he's convincing himself. Works as a set up to him going through with it anyway.

jokes.text: Andy: 'Let's ink my stink.'
jokes.setup: Andy has decided to go through with the tattoo despite his fear
jokes.punchline: 'Let's ink my stink' — a rallying cry that rhymes, uses slang, and refers to his butt with characteristic Andy flair
jokes.explanation: Four words, perfectly Andy. 'Let's ink my stink' rhymes, is filthy, is brave, and is delivered as a genuine war cry. It's the kind of line that becomes the episode's defining quote. Only Andy Bernard would say this — it's got his music-nerd rhyme sensibility applied to the most undignified situation possible. High quotability score fully warranted. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Andy: 'My heart belongs to music but my ass belongs to these people.'
jokes.setup: Andy is steeling himself before the tattoo
jokes.punchline: Andy's 'meaningful' declaration reframes corporate submission as romantic sacrifice — his ass as a love offering to his employees
jokes.explanation: The parallel structure ('My heart belongs to X but my ass belongs to Y') is a perfect comedic sentence. The word 'ass' disrupts what sounds like it's going to be an earnest declaration. The sentiment is also genuinely Andy — he means it. This line captures his character: romantic, performative, and ridiculous. Among the most quotable lines in the episode. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Tattoo artist: 'Uh, you can keep your pants on actually. If you just drop them down a bit that'd be great.' Andy: 'They are already off my good sir.'
jokes.setup: The tattoo is about to begin; the artist gives a routine instruction
jokes.punchline: Andy has already removed his pants entirely — he's committed so hard to the bit that he's gone further than required
jokes.explanation: 'They are already off my good sir' is a great line — the formality of 'my good sir' applied to announcing he's pantless is perfect Andy. His over-commitment to the bit (fully removing pants when only a slight drop was needed) is pure character comedy. The tattoo artist's deadpan preference for pants adds to the cringe.

jokes.text: Andy: 'I think down's better. Sweating pretty heavily down there.'
jokes.setup: The tattoo artist prefers Andy keep his pants on or just drop them slightly
jokes.punchline: Andy advocates for full-down pants by noting he's 'sweating pretty heavily down there' — an overshare that makes everything worse
jokes.explanation: The detail of the sweat is unnecessary information that Andy volunteers — classic overshare cringe comedy. 'Sweating pretty heavily down there' as justification for being more exposed is grimly funny.

jokes.text: Andy: 'This is where I grin and bear it.' [cotton swab touches him] 'Ow, ow!' Artist: 'That was just a cotton swab.' Andy: 'Invest in softer cotton, sir.'
jokes.setup: Andy announces he will bravely endure the tattoo needle
jokes.punchline: He immediately screams at a cotton swab — then, rather than accept defeat, critiques the quality of the cotton
jokes.explanation: Exceptional structure. The setup ('grin and bear it') creates a clear expectation of stoicism; the cotton swab deflates it immediately; then Andy's pivot to criticizing the cotton rather than accepting his cowardice is the perfect Andy move. 'Invest in softer cotton, sir' is Andy's signature blend of formal language, entitlement, and total ridiculousness. This is among the best joke constructions in the episode. Justifies 8+.

jokes.text: Robert's confessional on why he chose Andy: 'Because he's all surface, uncomplicated. What you see is what you get. It could be a recipe for mediocrity, yes. But then again, it might just be why people fight for him.'
jokes.setup: Robert is explaining his choice of Andy
jokes.punchline: Robert's assessment is both a dismissal ('all surface, uncomplicated') and a backhanded compliment — the joke is that the best thing he can say about Andy is that he's simple enough for people to root for
jokes.explanation: This is comedy-drama — it's funnier on reflection than in the moment. Robert's damning praise ('he's all surface') framed as insight is very Robert California. 'A recipe for mediocrity' is a great phrase. Slightly lower impact because it's more poignant than laugh-out-loud funny.

jokes.text: The reveal of the completed tattoo: 'It's a Nard dog.' 'That's my nickity name! I love it!'
jokes.setup: The tattoo design was a baby coming out of a butt; the finished product is revealed
jokes.punchline: The tattoo shows Andy's own nickname ('Nard Dog') — the baby-from-butt design apparently became or was always going to become a Nard Dog image; Andy's genuine delight ('That's my nickity name! I love it!') is the emotional payoff
jokes.explanation: 'That's my nickity name! I love it!' is a great payoff. Andy's instant, genuine love for the tattoo — the thing he dreaded — is a perfect character moment. 'Nickity name' is a Nard Dog-ism that fits perfectly. The reveal also reframes the entire incentive arc: Andy accidentally got exactly what he needed, a symbol of his relationship with his team. The 'Pull up your pants' button after is a nice capper.

jokes.text: Robert California: 'There's something about an underdog that really inspires the unexceptional.'
jokes.setup: Robert is reflecting on Andy's leadership as Andy celebrates his new tattoo
jokes.punchline: Robert calls the office staff 'the unexceptional' — not as an insult he's trying to hide, but as an accurate category he's comfortable saying aloud
jokes.explanation: 'The unexceptional' as a noun phrase for the office staff is a perfectly Robert California sentence. It's technically a compliment to Andy (he inspires people) while being a devastating assessment of the people he inspires. The casual delivery of 'the unexceptional' as a descriptive category, not a slight, is what makes it Robert. Highly quotable. Justifies the 8.

jokes.text: Angela's ethical dilemma opening: 'Well, we could talk about an ethical dilemma I'm having. A coworker of mine is drinking caffeine while pregnant and I don't know if I should call social services about it.'
jokes.setup: Angela and Pam are having a seemingly friendly pregnancy conversation
jokes.punchline: Angela's 'ethical dilemma' is barely disguised — she's describing Pam — and threatening social services over herbal tea with 'trace amounts of coffee'
jokes.explanation: Angela's thinly veiled passive aggression is perfectly in character. The 'coworker of mine' framing when she's talking directly to Pam is textbook Angela Martin. The nuclear escalation ('call social services') for trace coffee amounts is the comedic exaggeration that makes it funny rather than just catty.

jokes.text: Pam: 'Angela, that's pretty transparently me.' Angela: 'Maybe.'
jokes.setup: Angela has presented an obviously-Pam scenario as a hypothetical
jokes.punchline: Pam directly names the transparency; Angela's 'Maybe' is the perfect non-denial denial — she neither confirms nor retreats
jokes.explanation: 'Maybe' as Angela's total response is perfectly Angela — a one-word non-apology that concedes nothing. The economy is excellent. 'Maybe' here is funnier than any longer response could be.

jokes.text: Jim: 'Yeah. I think you should call social services.' Angela: 'I already did.'
jokes.setup: Pam has explained she's only drinking herbal tea with trace coffee; Jim sarcastically agrees with Angela
jokes.punchline: Angela has already called social services — she didn't need Jim's permission or even to finish the conversation
jokes.explanation: Episode-closing joke and one of the best in the episode. Jim's sarcasm ('Yeah, I think you should call social services') is immediately destroyed by Angela's flat 'I already did.' The pre-emptive action, the casual delivery, and the fact that Angela has already escalated to an extreme over trace amounts of coffee in herbal tea is devastating character comedy. It's earned — Angela has been established as vindictive, paranoid, and self-righteous. 'I already did' is four syllables of perfect characterization. Justifies 8.5+ across the board.

tmdb_overview: After Robert California challenges the Dunder Mifflin staffers to double their sales, Andy, taking matters into his own hands, creates an incentive program. Eventually, he promises to tattoo himself if the staff doubles their sales. Meanwhile, Pam strikes up an unlikely friendship with Angela, both of whom are pregnant.
